tips.title: Both paths start the same
tips.body: Every star begins **Nebula → Protostar → Main sequence star**. Only **after the main sequence** do the two paths separate, and which one it takes is decided by the **size of the star**. Learn the shared half once.

tips.title: Iron is the dividing line
tips.body: Fusion in stars makes elements **up to iron**. **Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova**, and the explosion **distributes them throughout the universe**. If a question mentions gold or uranium, the answer involves a supernova.

tips.title: A star is a balance, not a thing at rest
tips.body: A main sequence star is in **equilibrium**: **gravitational collapse** pulling inwards is balanced by **expansion due to fusion energy** pushing outwards. It is stable **because** the two are equal, not because nothing is happening.

tips.title: Changing velocity, unchanged speed
tips.body: In a circular orbit, **gravity changes the velocity but not the speed**. Velocity includes **direction**, and the direction is constantly turning; the **speed** — how fast — stays the same. This is a vector point, and it is examined.

tips.title: Faster orbit means smaller radius
tips.body: For a **stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes**. A satellite moving **faster** orbits at a **smaller** radius; slower means further out. Questions give you one and ask for the other.

why.matters:
Every atom in you heavier than hydrogen was made inside a star, and the star that made it is not the Sun. This topic is the life story that explains that: gravity gathers a cloud, fusion lights it, the two hold each other in balance for billions of years, and how it ends depends only on how big it was.

The same gravity that builds a star keeps the Moon, the planets and every satellite in orbit, which is why orbits are in the topic too.

examples.title: The gold in a ring
examples.body:
Fusion in a star builds heavier nuclei out of lighter ones, and it can only go as far as **iron**. So the calcium in your bones and the carbon in every cell were made in a star that died before the Sun was born.

Anything heavier than iron needs more than a star can give. It is made in the seconds of a **supernova**, the explosion that ends a star much more massive than the Sun. The gold in a ring and the uranium in a power station came through one. The hydrogen in water is the exception: it has been here since the beginning.

examples.title: Why the Sun is not a bonfire
examples.body:
A fire burns fast, then dies down. The Sun has held the same steady output for billions of years, and the reason is the equilibrium the specification describes: **gravity** pulling every part of it inwards against the **expansion** driven by fusion energy pushing out.

The balance corrects itself. If fusion slackened, gravity would squeeze the core smaller and hotter, and fusion would pick up again. If fusion ran too hard, the core would swell and cool, and fusion would ease. A main sequence star is a thermostat, not a flame, and it stays lit until the hydrogen in its core runs out.

boxes.title: Gravity pulls in
boxes.body: Every part of the star's mass is pulled towards the centre.

boxes.title: Fusion pushes out
boxes.body: Energy from fusion in the core expands the star against gravity.

boxes.title: If fusion slackens
boxes.body: Gravity wins a little: the core is squeezed hotter, and fusion picks up.

boxes.title: If fusion runs hot
boxes.body: Expansion wins a little: the core swells and cools, and fusion eases.

visual.alt: Four boxes showing a main sequence star's balance: gravity pulling inwards against expansion from fusion energy, and how either side correcting the other keeps the star steady

examples.title: Why the satellite dish never has to move
examples.body:
A dish on a wall points at one spot in the sky for years, yet the satellite it points at is in orbit, falling round the Earth. It stays put because of the specification's rule for a stable orbit: the higher the orbit, the slower the speed and the longer one lap takes.

A space station a few hundred kilometres up laps in about ninety minutes. A satnav satellite at 20 000 km takes about 12 hours. Put a satellite about 36 000 km up and one lap takes 24 hours, one turn of the Earth beneath it. From the ground it hangs still, so the dish is bolted on.

steps.title: The solar system
steps.body:
**Within our solar system there is one star, the Sun**, plus the **eight planets** and the **dwarf planets** that orbit around the Sun.

**Natural satellites — the moons that orbit planets — are also part of the solar system.**

**Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.** A galaxy is an enormous collection of stars, and the Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of them. The scale is worth holding on to: the Sun is one ordinary star among a vast number, in one galaxy among a vast number.

**How the Sun formed.** *The Sun was formed from a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) pulled together by gravitational attraction.*

That is the beginning of every star, not just ours. A **nebula** is a cloud of dust and gas, and **gravity** pulls it together. As the material falls inwards it becomes **denser and hotter**, because the particles collide more and more often.

**When it gets hot enough, fusion begins.** The specification puts it as: at the start of a star's life cycle, **the dust and gas drawn together by gravity causes fusion reactions**. Hydrogen nuclei are forced close enough together to fuse, and the star begins to shine.

**Then the star becomes stable**, and the reason is a balance — which is the next step.

steps.title: Why a star is stable
steps.body:
**A main sequence star is in equilibrium**, and the specification states what is being balanced:

> **Fusion reactions lead to an equilibrium between the gravitational collapse of a star and the expansion of a star due to fusion energy.**

**Two opposing effects.** **Gravity** pulls all the star's mass **inwards**, trying to collapse it. The **energy released by fusion** in the core pushes **outwards**, trying to expand it.

**While the two are equal, the star is stable** and stays the same size. This is the **main sequence**, and a star spends most of its life in it.

**The star is not at rest.** It is stable **because** two very large effects are cancelling, not because nothing is happening. That distinction is what "equilibrium" means, and questions test whether you understand it.

**Why the balance eventually fails.** Fusion needs fuel. When the **hydrogen in the core begins to run out**, the outward push from fusion **weakens** — and gravity, which never weakens, starts to win. The core contracts, which heats it further, and the star's outer layers **expand**.

**That is why a star leaves the main sequence**, and it is the moment the two life cycles separate. What happens next depends on one thing: **the size of the star**.

steps.title: Where the elements come from
steps.body:
**Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements.** Every atom heavier than hydrogen was made inside a star.

**Fusion builds heavier nuclei from lighter ones.** A main sequence star fuses hydrogen into helium. As it ages and its core gets hotter, heavier elements can be fused in turn — carbon, oxygen, and so on up the list.

**But fusion in a star stops at iron.** Fusing nuclei heavier than iron does not release energy; it **absorbs** it. So a star cannot power itself by making anything heavier, and the building stops there.

**Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.** The explosion of a massive star provides conditions violent enough to force those heavier nuclei together even though the process takes energy in rather than giving it out.

**The explosion of a massive star (supernova) distributes the elements throughout the universe.** The material is thrown out across space, where it can become part of new nebulae — and so of new stars and planets.

**The consequence is worth stating plainly.** The carbon in living things, the oxygen in the air, the iron in blood, and the gold and uranium in the ground were all made in stars, and the heaviest of them in exploding ones. The Earth exists because earlier stars lived and died first.

**For the exam:** *made in a star* covers elements **up to iron**; *made in a supernova* covers everything **heavier**. And the supernova is also what **spreads** them.

steps.title: Orbits
steps.body:
**Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites — both natural and artificial — to maintain their circular orbits.**

**Planets, moons and artificial satellites** are alike in that all **orbit** something under **gravity**. They differ in what they orbit and where they came from: **planets** orbit the **Sun**, **moons** are **natural satellites** orbiting **planets**, and **artificial satellites** are **made by people** and put into orbit deliberately, usually around the Earth.

**Changing velocity, unchanged speed.** For a circular orbit, **the force of gravity can lead to a changing velocity but an unchanged speed**.

This depends on a distinction that is easy to miss. **Speed** is how fast something is going. **Velocity** is speed **together with direction**. In a circular orbit the object is constantly **changing direction** — gravity pulls it towards the centre, bending its path into a circle — so its **velocity is always changing** even though its **speed** never does.

**Gravity acts at right angles to the motion**, which is why it turns the object without speeding it up or slowing it down.

**Speed and radius are linked.** For a **stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes**.

A satellite moving **faster** needs a **smaller** orbital radius; one moving **slower** orbits **further out**. Closer to the Earth, gravity is stronger, and a stronger pull is needed to bend a faster path into a circle.

**So you cannot choose speed and height independently.** Pick the height and the speed is fixed; pick the speed and the height is fixed. If a satellite's speed changes and its radius does not, the orbit is **no longer stable** — it will spiral inwards or move outwards until the two match again.

check.prompt: In a stable circular orbit, what happens to a satellite's speed and velocity?
options: The speed is unchanged but the velocity changes
Both the speed and the velocity change
Both the speed and the velocity stay the same
The speed changes but the velocity is unchanged
check.solution: Gravity acts **at right angles to the motion**, so it changes the **direction** without changing how fast the object goes. Since **velocity includes direction**, the velocity is constantly changing while the **speed is unchanged**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Learn the shared beginning once.** Every star runs **Nebula → Protostar → Main sequence star**. Only after the main sequence do the paths separate, and it is the **size of the star** that decides which one it takes.

**Describe the equilibrium as a balance of two named effects.** **Gravitational collapse** inwards against **expansion due to fusion energy** outwards. Saying a star is "stable" without naming both sides leaves the marks on the table.

**Explain why the balance fails.** Fusion needs **fuel**. When the hydrogen runs low the outward push weakens, while **gravity does not weaken at all** — so gravity wins and the star leaves the main sequence. That asymmetry is the whole reason stars have a life cycle.

**Use iron as the dividing line.** Fusion in stars makes elements **up to iron**; **heavier than iron requires a supernova**, because fusing beyond iron **absorbs** energy rather than releasing it. Then add the second half: the supernova also **distributes** those elements through the universe.

**Do not give a Sun-sized star a supernova.** It becomes a **red giant**, then a **white dwarf**, then a **black dwarf**. Supernovae, neutron stars and black holes belong only to the **much more massive** path.

**Be exact about velocity and speed.** **Velocity includes direction**; speed does not. Gravity acts **at right angles** to the motion in a circular orbit, so it continually changes the **direction** — and therefore the velocity — while leaving the **speed** unchanged. This is a vector point, and a vague answer will not score.

**Link speed and radius the right way round.** **Faster means a smaller radius**; slower means further out. Closer in, gravity is stronger, and a stronger force is needed to bend a faster path into a circle. If the speed changes and the radius does not, the orbit is **not stable**.

**Keep the categories straight.** **Planets** orbit the Sun; **moons are natural satellites** orbiting planets; **artificial satellites** are made by people. All three are held in orbit by **gravity**, which is the similarity the specification asks for alongside the distinctions.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The solar system has **one star** (the Sun), **eight planets**, dwarf planets and **moons**.
- **Moons are natural satellites** orbiting planets.
- Our solar system is **a small part of the Milky Way galaxy**.
- The Sun formed from a **nebula** — dust and gas — pulled together by **gravitational attraction**.
- Gravity draws material together until it is hot enough for **fusion**.
- A star is in **equilibrium**: **gravitational collapse** balanced by **expansion due to fusion energy**.
- Both life cycles begin **Nebula → Protostar → Main sequence star**.
- **Sun-sized**: → **Red giant → White dwarf → Black dwarf**.
- **Much more massive**: → **Red super giant → Supernova → Neutron star or black hole**.
- The life cycle is **determined by the size of the star**.
- **Fusion produces all the naturally occurring elements**, up to **iron**.
- **Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova**.
- The **supernova distributes the elements throughout the universe**.
- **Gravity** provides the force maintaining **circular orbits**.
- In a circular orbit, **velocity changes but speed does not**.
- For a **stable orbit**, the **radius must change if the speed changes** — faster means closer.

questions.prompt: Describe the life cycle of a star the size of the Sun and of a star much more massive than the Sun, explaining what causes a star to be stable and why it eventually changes.
questions.skill: the life cycle of a star
questions.solution:
**Every star begins in the same way.** A **nebula** — a cloud of dust and gas — is **pulled together by gravitational attraction**. As the material falls inwards it becomes **denser and hotter**, forming a **protostar**.

When the protostar becomes hot enough, **fusion reactions begin** and it becomes a **main sequence star**. The specification puts it directly: at the start of a star's life cycle, **the dust and gas drawn together by gravity causes fusion reactions**.

**Why a main sequence star is stable.** Fusion reactions lead to an **equilibrium between the gravitational collapse of a star and the expansion of a star due to fusion energy**. Gravity pulls all the star's mass **inwards**; the energy released by fusion in the core pushes **outwards**. While the two are equal the star stays the same size, and it spends **most of its life** in this state.

It is worth being clear that the star is stable **because two enormous effects are cancelling**, not because nothing is happening inside it.

**Why the balance eventually fails.** Fusion requires **fuel**. As the hydrogen in the core runs low, the outward push from fusion **weakens** — but **gravity does not weaken at all**. That asymmetry means gravity eventually wins, the core contracts and heats further, and the outer layers expand. The star leaves the main sequence.

**What happens next is determined by the size of the star.**

**A star the size of the Sun** swells into a **red giant**. It then sheds its outer layers, leaving behind a hot, dense core called a **white dwarf**. With no fusion to sustain it, the white dwarf slowly cools and fades to a **black dwarf**. The end is quiet, with no explosion.

**A star much more massive than the Sun** instead becomes a **red super giant**. Because its mass is so much greater, gravity is far stronger, and when the balance fails the collapse is violent — the star explodes as a **supernova**. What remains at the centre is a **neutron star**, or, if the original star was massive enough, a **black hole**.

**One further consequence.** **Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements**, but only up to **iron**, because fusing anything heavier absorbs energy rather than releasing it. **Elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova**, and **the explosion distributes the elements throughout the universe** — where they can become part of new nebulae, and so of later stars and planets.

questions.prompt: Explain how gravity keeps satellites in orbit, and explain how a satellite in a circular orbit can have a changing velocity but a constant speed, and why its speed and orbital radius are linked.
questions.solution:
**Gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites — both natural and artificial — to maintain their circular orbits.** Without it there would be no orbit at all: the satellite would simply travel in a straight line and leave.

The crucial detail is the **direction** in which gravity acts. For a circular orbit, gravity pulls the satellite **towards the centre** of the body it orbits, which is at **right angles to its direction of motion** at every instant.

**How velocity can change while speed does not.** This depends on a distinction that is easy to skate over. **Speed** is simply how fast something is moving. **Velocity** is speed **together with direction** — it is a vector, and changing either part changes the velocity.

A satellite in a circular orbit is **constantly changing direction**: its path is being bent into a circle. So although it may be travelling at a steady 7,000 metres per second throughout, the **direction** of that motion is different at every moment. Its **velocity is therefore changing continuously**, even though its **speed is constant**.

The reason the speed does not change is that gravity acts **perpendicular to the motion**. A force in the direction of travel would speed the satellite up, and one against it would slow it down — but a force at right angles does neither. It only **turns** the satellite, which is exactly what is needed to hold it in a circle.

So the specification's statement that **the force of gravity can lead to changing velocity but unchanged speed** is not a paradox: it follows directly from velocity being a vector and gravity acting sideways.

**Why speed and radius are linked.** For a **stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes**. The two cannot be chosen independently.

The relationship runs in the direction that often feels backwards: a satellite moving **faster** orbits at a **smaller** radius, and one moving **slower** orbits **further out**. The reason is that gravity is **stronger closer in**, and a **stronger force** is exactly what is needed to bend a **faster** path into a circle. Further out, gravity is weaker, so only a slower path can be bent enough to close into an orbit.

**The consequence is practical.** If a satellite's speed increases while its radius stays the same, gravity is no longer sufficient to hold that path and the satellite moves **outwards**. If it slows, gravity is more than enough and it spirals **inwards**. In either case the orbit is **not stable** until speed and radius match one another again — which is why moving a satellite to a higher orbit requires **reducing** its orbital speed once it arrives.

examTechnique.body:
Both life cycles share **Nebula → Protostar → Main sequence star**; the **size of the star** decides the rest, and a **Sun-sized star never goes supernova**.

Describe stability as **gravitational collapse balanced by expansion from fusion energy**, and explain that the balance fails because **fuel runs out while gravity does not weaken**. Remember **iron** is the dividing line for element formation.
examinerErrors: Giving a Sun-sized star a supernova.
Saying a star is "stable" without naming both balanced effects.
Not explaining why the equilibrium eventually fails.
Saying all elements are made by fusion in stars.
Forgetting that the supernova also distributes the elements.
Saying a satellite's speed changes in a circular orbit.
Getting the speed and radius relationship the wrong way round.
Treating moons and artificial satellites as the same thing.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer learns the **shared beginning** once and knows the **size of the star** decides the rest, never giving a Sun-sized star a supernova. It describes equilibrium as **two named opposing effects** and explains the failure through an **asymmetry** — fuel runs out, gravity does not weaken. It uses **iron** as the dividing line, and adds that the supernova both **creates** the heavier elements and **distributes** them. On orbits it is exact about vectors: **velocity includes direction**, gravity acts **at right angles**, so direction changes and speed does not — and it gets **faster means closer** the right way round, explaining it by gravity being stronger further in.
